digest.top_line: RNI review: MA.20 10-yr DFS 82% vs 77%, EORTC 22922 72.1% vs 69.1%, no OS gain in either trial alone; breast nodal RT carries a review-only day.
digest.tldr: All five sources are narrative reviews, no new trial readouts. Breast carries the day: RNI (MA.20/EORTC 22922 DFS gains, pooled 1-2% 10-yr OS), ALND omission after Z0011/AMAROS, and response-adapted PMRT after NAC (ypN+ no-RT LRR ≥15%). Prostate urethral dose steering and liver SBRT BED ≥100 Gy10 (3-yr LC 93% vs 65%) round out RT technique.

sites.intro: Liver SBRT dose selection tracks BED and OAR distance; the evidence base stays single-arm and retrospective.

studies.name: SBRT for liver metastases (Seminars in Radiation Oncology review)
studies.tldr: BED ≥100 Gy10 tied to 3-year LC 93% vs 65% in liver mets; review maps fractionation to OAR distance and liver dose constraints.
details: 🔍 Narrative review, Seminars in Radiation Oncology 2023; no systematic search method stated in source
📊 Pooled analysis of 13 studies: 3-year LC 76% mets vs 86% primary liver tumors
📐 BED >100 Gy10 in mets: 3-year LC 93% vs 65%
📊 Single-fraction 35-40 Gy (BED 157.5-200 Gy10), median size 2.0 cm: 4-year LC 96.6%

details.text: 🔍 Proposed fractionation by tumor distance to OARs (non-cirrhotic liver)

rows: <1 cm from luminal GI or central biliary tree

details: 📊 HyTEC: rVdose ≥700cc <15-17Gy as a planning rule → G3+ toxicity 9.3%
🔗 SBRT vs RFA meta-analysis, 2238 pts: 2-year LC 84% vs 60% in liver mets studies, no OS difference
📊 CRC liver mets meta-analysis, 656 pts: 2-year LC 59%, OS 57%, G3+ liver toxicity 8.7%
⚠️ Central liver zone (2 cm shell around portal vein): caution, biliary stricture risk
⚠️ Evidence base is single-arm prospective and retrospective series with heterogeneous dose; constraints are conservative, not tolerance-derived
⚠️ Kress, RPA and CRC prognostic scores are retrospectively derived and not externally validated
studies.significance: The dose argument rests on one pooled analysis: BED above 100 Gy10 tracked with 3-year LC 93% vs 65% in mets, while primary liver tumors showed no gain above 100 Gy10. That separates the dose target for liver mets from HCC practice. For lesions near bowel or the central biliary tree, the review protracts fractionation rather than lowering BED.
studies.monday_clinic: In a non-cirrhotic pt with a liver metastasis abutting bowel or the central biliary tree, this supports protracted fractionation over a 3-fraction ablative course; it does not extend to cirrhotic livers, where the cited limits are tighter.

analysis_sections.label: Design
analysis_sections.body: Narrative **topic review** of liver SBRT for metastases. It covers prospective series, pooled analyses, prognostic scores, QOL, dose and fractionation, OAR tolerance and motion management. No search strategy or inclusion criteria are stated in the source.

analysis_sections.label: Radiotherapy
analysis_sections.body: Most series use **3-5 fractions** (range 1-6). When maximizing LC is the priority the review recommends **BED ≥100 Gy10 to the PTV**. Fractionation is chosen to respect OARs in priority order: luminal GI, central biliary tree, chest wall, then liver. An SIB with PRV is suggested for tumors 1-2 cm from OARs.

analysis_sections.label: Safety
analysis_sections.body: QUANTEC: MLD limits of **15 Gy in 3 fractions** and **20 Gy in 6 fractions** keep the risk of G3 liver enzyme toxicity under 20%. In 6-fraction SBRT, G3 liver enzyme risk was 0% at MLD ≤15Gy but 6-18% at MLD ≤21Gy, depending on D800cc, so MLD alone is insufficient.

analysis_sections.label: vs leading data
analysis_sections.body: Against RFA, a 2238-pt meta-analysis showed **2-year LC 84% vs 60%** favoring SBRT in liver mets studies, with **no OS difference** and G3+ toxicity <5% for both. MAESTRO, a randomized phase II trial of MR-guided adaptive vs ITV-based SBRT, is cited as the randomized technique question.

analysis_sections.label: Applies to
analysis_sections.body: Represents liver oligometastases, mostly non-cirrhotic, including unresectable colorectal liver metastases. Does not represent cirrhotic livers or HCC, for which the review cites tighter constraints and a different dose response.

analysis_sections.label: Limitations
analysis_sections.body: The BED >100 Gy10 threshold comes from a pooled analysis of published series, open to selection by lesion size and location. Several cited constraints are borrowed from the ASTRO guideline for liver primaries, not derived in metastases.

analysis_sections.label: Discussion
analysis_sections.body: The review positions SBRT for lesions percutaneous ablation handles poorly: periampullary, perihilar, subcapsular, perivascular or large tumors. Optimal dose and fractionation remain **unknown**, with no consensus guideline. Whether CRC histology is radioresistant at sufficiently high dose is unresolved.

studies.interpretation:
The practical weight of this review rests on its dose-selection framework, and it helps to see how thin the evidence under that framework is. The claim that liver metastases need more dose than primary liver tumors comes from a pooled analysis of 13 published series. Metastases had lower 3-year LC than primaries (76% vs 86%), and lesions treated above a BED of 100 Gy10 did better than those below it (93% vs 65%). The finding is biologically plausible and consistent with the single-fraction phase 1 experience. But it is a cross-series comparison, and the confounding runs in a predictable direction. Lesions that can safely reach a BED above 100 Gy10 are the small ones far from bowel and the central biliary tree, and the review itself lists smaller tumor volume as an independent predictor of LC. Part of the dose effect may therefore be a size and location effect. A reader should treat 100 Gy10 as a reasonable planning target for a lesion that allows it, not as a proven threshold below which control collapses.

The fractionation tiers keyed to OAR distance follow from that reasoning. They are an argument for keeping BED high by protracting delivery, rather than de-escalating dose when anatomy is unfavorable. That is sensible, but the review offers no outcome data for the 10-15 fraction tier in liver metastases. Its support comes from a review of external beam RT and from dose-escalated pancreas practice. For a lesion within 1 cm of duodenum, the reader is borrowing technique from pancreas SBRT, and should say so when counseling.

The SBRT vs RFA comparison deserves the most caution. A meta-analysis favoring SBRT on 2-year LC with no OS difference is what one would expect when nonrandomized cohorts are compared. Tumor size, location relative to vessels and referral pattern all differ between the two modalities, and the heat-sink effect the review describes biases RFA failures toward exactly the perivascular lesions SBRT is often chosen for. The LC gap may be real, but its size cannot be read from pooled observational data. The absence of an OS difference is the more defensible finding, because local therapy for one lesion rarely drives survival when extrahepatic progression dominates.

On toxicity, the review is candid that liver SBRT constraints are conservative values that proved safe on trials, not tolerance doses. Several of the most-cited limits come from the ASTRO guideline for liver primaries. Applying them to a non-cirrhotic oligometastatic liver is likely conservative rather than dangerous. The point the review makes well is that mean liver dose alone does not predict enzyme toxicity once the spared critical volume is small.

What the review does not settle is the question that matters most for an RT reader: which patients with liver oligometastases gain survival from ablation at all. The prognostic scores it cites are retrospective and unvalidated. Until randomized data separate patient selection from treatment effect, the dose and constraint guidance here is a sound way to deliver SBRT safely, not evidence of when to deliver it.

significance_by_specialty.radonc: BED above 100 Gy10 tracked with 3-year LC 93% vs 65% in mets but not in primary liver tumors, so the dose target differs from HCC practice. Near bowel or the central biliary tree, the review protracts to 10-15 fractions instead of lowering BED.

details: 📊 Pooled MA.20 + EORTC 22922 + French IMC trial: absolute 1-2% 10-yr OS gain with RNI

details.text: 🔗 EBCTCG PMRT meta-analysis, 1-3 LN+, at 10 yr

subdetails: Coronary events rose 7.4% per Gy mean heart dose (2168 women, 1958-2001)
Retrospective: CAD 18% with vs 7% without IMC fields, P=0.01

ACOSOG Z0011 (N=891, cT1-2N0, 1-2 SLN+): LRR 1.6% SLND vs 3.1% ALND, P=0.11

⚠️ SLN microsectioning converts 10-50% of negative SLNs: trial-era pN1 is not modern pN1
🔍 Proposed RNI risk modifiers: LNR, premenopausal age, grade III, LVI, ECE, subtype, Oncotype RS

studies.significance: The transferable detail is target volume: MA.20 treated IMC, SCV and level III axilla after BCS in a cohort roughly 85% 1-3 node-positive, while EORTC 22922 treated IMC plus medial SCV with 44.4% node-negative in the RNI arm. Both DFS gains (82% vs 77%; 72.1% vs 69.1%) support nodal fields in higher-risk pN1, with IMC coverage planned against cardiac dose.

analysis_sections.label: Radiotherapy
analysis_sections.body: Target volumes differ by trial: **MA.20** treated the undissected axilla, IMC (first 3 intercostal spaces) and SCV; **EORTC 22922** treated IMC and medial SCV. Z0011-era **high tangents** cover most of level I/II but not level III or SCV.

analysis_sections.label: Safety
analysis_sections.body: RNI adds cardiopulmonary toxicity and lymphedema risk, worst after complete ALND. Coronary events rose **7.4% per Gy** mean heart dose in a 1958-2001 series, and a retrospective series showed CAD **18% vs 7%** with vs without IMC fields (P=0.01).

analysis_sections.label: vs leading data
analysis_sections.body: EBCTCG PMRT data in 1-3 node disease frame the debate; **MA.20** and **EORTC 22922** test it with CT-era RT. AMAROS and ACOSOG Z0011 recast the axilla as an RT target after limited SLN disease.

analysis_sections.label: Applies to
analysis_sections.body: Represents stage II, pN1 or high-risk pN0 breast cancer after BCS or mastectomy. Does not represent cT1-3N1 disease converting to ypT0N0 after neoadjuvant chemotherapy, which the authors route to NSABP-B51.

analysis_sections.label: Limitations
analysis_sections.body: Narrative, not systematic; cardiac evidence mixes pre-CT-era and retrospective series. Trial-era pN1 differs from today's microsectioned, SLN-staged pN1, so absolute gains may not transfer.

analysis_sections.label: Discussion
analysis_sections.body: Authors favor RNI for advanced and **high-risk stage II** disease and ask that grade, subtype, nodal burden and extent of axillary surgery guide stage I-II decisions. **Recurrence-score-guided RNI** is proposed but untested prospectively.

studies.interpretation:
The review's core claim is that RNI in pN1 disease rests on two trials that answered slightly different questions, and that their modest absolute gains have to be re-weighed against a population that has changed since they accrued. MA.20 was almost entirely a 1-3 node, breast-conservation, chemotherapy-treated cohort with level III axilla in the field. EORTC 22922 mixed mastectomy and BCS, enrolled a large node-negative fraction on the basis of tumor location, and treated a narrower IMC plus medial SCV volume. That both showed DFS and distant DFS gains without an individual OS gain is the consistent finding. The pooled analysis with the French IMC trial is what supplies the absolute 1-2% OS figure, and that figure carries the review's argument that RNI is not merely a locoregional intervention.

The weaker part of the argument is transfer. The authors identify two forces eroding the trial-era baseline: SLN microsectioning and immunohistochemistry, which convert 10 to 50% of negative nodes to positive and so dilute today's pN1 with low-burden disease, and the move from ALND to SLN biopsy alone, which changes what is left undissected and therefore what RNI is treating. A reader should expect the absolute benefit in a modern, micrometastasis-enriched pN1 population to be smaller than the trial numbers, not equal to them, although the review cannot say by how much.

Z0011 sits awkwardly in this frame, and the review is candid about it. The SLN-alone arm's low regional recurrence is often cited as evidence the axilla can be left alone, yet among those with detailed RT records roughly half received high tangents and 19% received dedicated nodal fields. That makes Z0011 partly an unplanned nodal RT trial, and it limits how far it can support omission of nodal RT. AMAROS is the cleaner comparison, axillary RT against completion dissection, with less lymphedema and low axillary recurrence in both arms, though it was not powered for non-inferiority.

On toxicity, the cardiac data cited combine a pre-CT-era dose-response series with a retrospective IMC-field series, so they argue for heart-sparing IMC planning rather than for dropping the IMC. The proposed selectors (nodal ratio, age, grade, LVI, ECE, subtype, recurrence score) are reasonable but none has been tested as an RNI selector. The Danish PMRT tissue analysis, in which the OS benefit was confined to ER/PR-positive, HER2-negative disease, cuts against using a luminal subtype to de-escalate nodal RT.

The review dates from 2017. Its post-neoadjuvant guidance points to NSABP-B51 and Alliance A011202 as the trials that would settle RNI after nodal response and after SLN positivity following NAC. Both were open when it was written, so that section frames the question rather than answering it, and should be read against those trials' own reports.

significance_by_specialty.radonc: Target volume is what transfers: MA.20 treated IMC, SCV and level III axilla after BCS, EORTC 22922 treated IMC plus medial SCV. DFS gains in both support nodal fields in higher-risk pN1, and the CAD 18% vs 7% IMC series argues for heart-sparing IMC planning, not omission.
significance_by_specialty.surgonc: Extent of axillary surgery now feeds the RNI decision. AMAROS put axillary RT against ALND (5-yr axillary recurrence 1.19% vs 0.43%, less lymphedema), and Z0011's SLN-alone arm had LRR 1.6% with many receiving high tangents, so surgical choice and nodal field design are coupled.

Is RNI needed after nodal pCR following neoadjuvant chemotherapy?

studies.name: Radiation decisions after neoadjuvant chemotherapy and mastectomy
studies.tldr: No randomised post-NAC PMRT data: retrospective MDACC/NSABP series put ypN+ LRR without RT at ≥15%, cT1–T2 ypN0 <10%, supporting response-adapted PMRT.
details: 🔍 Lancet Oncol 2012 Personal View; Medline/Embase searched to October 2011
⚠️ No randomised PMRT-vs-none data after NAC + mastectomy; evidence is retrospective or non-randomised
🔍 NSABP B-18/B-27 prohibited PMRT after mastectomy, giving a no-RT LRR baseline

details.text: 📊 MDACC 676 pts post-NAC mastectomy, 10-yr LRR without vs with PMRT
📊 MDACC no-PMRT 5-yr LRR by clinical T stage and pathological nodal status

details: 📊 NSABP B-18/B-27 8-yr LRF without PMRT: 14.9% ypN+ (n=447) vs 5.9% pCR + ypN0 (n=68)

details.text: 📊 Response after NAC: LRR outcomes without vs with PMRT
📊 Clinical T3N0 (MDACC, n=162), 5-yr LRR without vs with PMRT
subdetails: NSABP no-RT 10-yr LRF: 14.0% ypN+, 11.8% ypN0 residual breast, 6.2% ypN0 pCR

details.text: 📊 Age <35, cStage IIA–IIIC (MDACC, n=107), without vs with PMRT

details: 🔗 EBCTCG upfront-surgery node+: 5-yr isolated LRR 22.8% vs 5.8%, 15-yr BC mortality 60.1% vs 54.7%
⚠️ MDACC cohorts overlap across publications and span eras of changing staging, imaging, chemo and surgery
⚠️ Mostly doxorubicin-based NAC; one trastuzumab-based series converted 74% of cN+ to ypN0
🔍 RAPCHEM (NCT01279304): non-randomised, cT1–T2 cN+ → ypN0, no PMRT after mastectomy, 5-yr LRR
studies.significance: The omission case rests on small denominators: NSABP pCR + ypN0 (n=68) had 5.9% 8-yr LRF without PMRT, MDACC cT1–2 ypN0 (n=19) 5%. Clinical T3N0 converting to ypN0 is the contested cell (MDACC 14% vs 2%, p=0.06; NSABP 6.2% and 11.8%), so chest wall and nodal RT stay individualized there.
studies.monday_clinic: In clinical T1–T2 disease that is ypN0 after NAC and mastectomy, these data support discussing PMRT omission; they do not extend to clinical T3–T4, N2–N3, or ypN+ disease, where retrospective series favor PMRT.

analysis_sections.label: Design
analysis_sections.body: Lancet Oncol 2012 Personal View from MD Anderson radiation and surgical oncology authors. Medline and Embase searched to **October 2011**; inflammatory breast cancer excluded.

analysis_sections.label: vs leading data
analysis_sections.body: Upfront-mastectomy PMRT benefit comes from the Danish and Canadian randomised trials and the EBCTCG meta-analysis, all predating routine NAC. **Pathological extent after NAC carries higher risk**: with ≥4 involved nodes, MDACC 5-yr LRR was **53% vs 23%** neoadjuvant vs upfront surgery (p<0.001).

analysis_sections.label: Applies to
analysis_sections.body: Represents non-inflammatory, non-metastatic breast cancer treated with NAC and mastectomy. Does not represent inflammatory breast cancer or breast-conserving surgery.

analysis_sections.label: Limitations
analysis_sections.body: MDACC series overlap across publications and span eras of evolving staging, imaging, chemo and surgery. NSABP pts were earlier stage than MDACC pts: only **35%** had clinical nodal involvement at diagnosis.

analysis_sections.label: Discussion
analysis_sections.body: Authors propose response-adapted PMRT: LRR **at least 15%** without RT in ypN+ supports PMRT, **<10%** in cT1–T2 ypN0 supports omission. Clinical stage III with pCR is **unsettled**, with MDACC and Le Scodan pointing in opposite directions.

studies.interpretation:
Published in 2012, this Personal View is best read as the hypothesis document for response-adapted PMRT rather than an evidence base for it. Its central argument is that the upfront-surgery rules (four or more involved nodes, pathological stage III) cannot be transplanted to the post-NAC setting, because chemotherapy changes what the pathology report means. The strongest evidence offered is the MDACC comparison of neoadjuvant and upfront cohorts treated without RT, where four or more involved nodes carried 53% vs 23% 5-yr LRR. Residual nodal disease after NAC marks chemoresistant biology, not just burden, so the same nodal count signals a worse tumour.

The addition argument is stronger than the omission argument, and the asymmetry matters. The case for PMRT in clinical T3–T4, N2–N3 and ypN+ disease rests on large absolute LRR differences in a 676-patient MDACC series, consistent in direction with the Danish and Canadian randomised trials and the EBCTCG overview in the upfront setting. The authors note the irradiated groups carried more adverse features, which would bias against finding a benefit rather than toward it. The case for omission rests on small denominators: 68 NSABP pts with pCR and ypN0, 19 MDACC pts in the cT1–T2 ypN0 stratum, 30 stage II pCR pts with no events in either arm. Low event rates in small groups leave wide uncertainty, and the low-risk NSABP cohorts were earlier stage than the MDACC experience, so part of what defines the low-risk group is who entered the trials.

The contested cells are clinical stage III with pCR and clinical T3N0 converting to ypN0. MDACC and Le Scodan disagree on the first, and the disagreement cannot be resolved from these data: both are retrospective with few events, and the Le Scodan adjusted HR of 0.37 has a 95% CI of 0.09–1.61. For cT3N0 ypN0, MDACC reports 14% vs 2% (p=0.06), while NSABP no-RT rates are 11.8% with residual breast disease and 6.2% with pCR. The gap between institutions in untreated cT3N0 LRR is the tell: baseline risk differs across referral populations by more than the effect being estimated, which is exactly the situation in which retrospective comparison misleads.

For a radiation oncologist the durable contribution is the two-axis framework, clinical stage at presentation plus nodal response, and the insistence on documenting pre-NAC nodal extent with ultrasound of all regional basins and FNA so the later decision has an anchor. What the review cannot address is the modern regimen. The cohorts received doxorubicin-based NAC, and the authors flag that trastuzumab-based therapy converted 74% of cN+ pts to ypN0 in one series, enlarging precisely the group whose omission data are thinnest. It also addresses whether to irradiate, not what to irradiate: chest wall vs regional nodal coverage after nodal conversion is never separated.

The authors' own conclusion, that RAPCHEM and a randomised Alliance proposal are needed before omission becomes routine, is the correct read. The omission recommendation would be wrong if ypN0 status after effective NAC under-calls residual nodal disease, or if biology-driven systemic therapy shifts baseline LRR in ways that make these historical no-RT rates unrepresentative.

significance_by_specialty.radonc: The omission case rests on small denominators: NSABP pCR + ypN0 (n=68) had 5.9% 8-yr LRF without PMRT, MDACC cT1–2 ypN0 (n=19) 5%. Clinical T3N0 converting to ypN0 is the contested cell (MDACC 14% vs 2%, p=0.06), so chest wall and nodal RT stay individualized there.

studies.name: Urinary toxicity from prostate radiotherapy: mechanisms, mitigation, management
studies.tldr: Narrative review: urethral dose steering (FLAME-derived D0.1 cm³ <105% Rx; SBRT Dmax <107% → est. 7.7% late moderate GU) is the main mitigation lever.
details: 🔍 Narrative review, Lancet Oncol 2022; PubMed 1995 to April 2022, no quantitative synthesis

details.text: 📊 Urinary toxicity by anatomic site and phase
subdetails: Bladder mucosa: acute irritation; late fibrosis, contracture, telangiectasia, bleeding
Prostatic/membranous urethra: acute irritation; subacute ulceration; late stricture
Prostate: acute swelling → obstruction; late fibrosis → fewer obstructive symptoms
Trigone: acute irritation; late neurogenic chronic urgency

details: 📊 Acute irritative symptoms in ~50%; typically resolve within 4–6 weeks post-RT
🔗 Dutch RCT: 68 → 78 Gy conventional dose escalation did not raise urinary toxicity
📊 FLAME DIL boost: bDFS 92% vs 85%, HR 0.45 (0.28–0.71), p<0.001
📐 FLAME dosimetric analysis: urethral dose-effect, no clear threshold; urethra D0.1 cm³ <105% Rx recommended
📐 SBRT 40 Gy/5 fx: urethral Dmax <107% → estimated late moderate GU 7.7% (23 trials, 2232 pts)
📊 MSKCC phase 1 at 40 Gy/5 fx without urethral sparing: late moderate-severe GU 12 of 53 (34.3%)

rows: 19 or 20 Gy/2 fx + EBRT 46 Gy/23 fx
Acute G2 26.6%; late G≥2 6.3% at 36 mo
Urethra PRV max D0.1 cm³ ≤38.78 Gy

details: ⚠️ Table 1 series differ in grading, follow-up and reporter; rates don't rank modalities
🔗 ASCENDE-RT stricture: 18.4% of 188 brachy boost vs 5.2% of 195 EBRT, p<0.001
⚠️ Anticoagulants: 4-yr G3+ bleeding 15.5% vs 3.6% (single institution, 568 pts)
📊 Post-RT TURP incontinence: 18% (7 of 38) post-brachy; 27% (30 of 111) post-EBRT/brachy
📊 Secondary malignancy after EBRT: absolute increase 0.1% to 3.8% (21 studies), higher in younger pts

details.text: 🔍 Ongoing randomised SBRT trials with urethral steering/sparing (review Table 2, status as of 2022)

rows: Virtual HDR boost 20 Gy/2 fx + EBRT 36 Gy/12 fx

studies.significance: The planning numbers are the transferable part: urethra D0.1 cm³ <105% of prescription from the FLAME dosimetric analysis, and Dmax <107% at 40 Gy/5 fx tied to an estimated 7.7% late moderate GU rate. Sparing below prescription stays conditional on MRI or PSMA PET localisation with tumor clear of the urethra.
studies.monday_clinic: In men with moderate-to-high IPSS or obstructive urodynamics before prostate RT, this supports weighing pre-emptive TURP; it argues against TURP early after RT for persistent obstructive symptoms, where incontinence reached 18% (7 of 38) and 27% (30 of 111) in two series.

analysis_sections.label: Design
analysis_sections.body: Narrative **review** (Lancet Oncol, December 2022) from an Australian radiation oncology and urology group. PubMed search 1995 to April 2022 plus the authors' files; English only, **no quantitative synthesis**.

analysis_sections.label: Radiotherapy
analysis_sections.body: FLAME-derived constraint: urethra **D0.1 cm³ <105%** of the prostate prescription. For 40 Gy/5 fx SBRT, urethral **Dmax <107%** was estimated to give late moderate GU toxicity of **7.7%**. HDR brachytherapy has no urethral consensus; one ABS guideline lists **11 different constraints**.

analysis_sections.label: Safety
analysis_sections.body: Acute irritative symptoms in **~50%**, resolving within 4–6 weeks. Stricture risk rises with brachytherapy boost and salvage post-RP RT; 4-yr G3+ bleeding was **15.5% on anticoagulants vs 3.6%** without.

analysis_sections.label: vs leading data
analysis_sections.body: FLAME showed a DIL boost improved bDFS (**HR 0.45**, 95% CI 0.28–0.71) without an overall rise in moderate-to-severe GU toxicity. ASCENDE-RT is the counterpart for brachytherapy dose escalation, with stricture **18.4% vs 5.2%**. PROTECT showed RT-related QoL detriment regressing over 12 months.

analysis_sections.label: Discussion
analysis_sections.body: The thesis is that cure and urinary function need not trade off if urethral dose, image guidance, ADT cytoreduction and **early salvage over adjuvant RT** are used. Urethral sparing below prescription stays conditional on reliable MRI or PSMA PET localisation with tumor away from the urethra.

analysis_sections.label: Limitations
analysis_sections.body: Most toxicity series are retrospective and physician-graded, and CTCAE/RTOG scales under-capture chronic urgency. The reassurance on relapse with urethral sparing is qualitative, with no event counts given.

analysis_sections.label: Applies to
analysis_sections.body: Represents men receiving definitive or post-prostatectomy RT for localized prostate cancer. Does not represent anorectal or cervical pelvic RT, which the review mentions but does not address.

studies.interpretation:
The useful argument in this review is that urinary toxicity from prostate RT is now partly a planning variable rather than a fixed cost of cure. The evidence it assembles for that claim is uneven, and a reader should weight each piece separately. The strongest is FLAME: a randomised focal-boost trial that improved bDFS (HR 0.45) without a clear rise in moderate-to-severe GU toxicity, and whose dosimetric analysis exposed a urethral dose-effect relationship precisely because the protocol set no urethral limit. That is the one place where a urethral constraint (D0.1 cm³ under 105% of the prostate prescription) comes from randomised-trial patients, although the dose-toxicity analysis is itself retrospective and found no clear threshold.

The SBRT side rests on weaker ground. The 7.7% expected late moderate GU toxicity with urethral Dmax under 107% at 40 Gy/5 fx is a modelled estimate from a systematic review of 23 prospective trials, not an observed rate in a cohort planned to that constraint. It is set against the MSKCC phase 1 experience without urethral sparing, a contrast across different trials, delineation methods (catheter or MRI) and constraint definitions. The Table 1 series point the same way: late G2 rates of 4% in several 5-fraction urethral-sparing cohorts sit beside 31% at 7 years after HDR boost, but the series differ in grading tool, follow-up and whether toxicity was physician or patient reported. Those same reporting problems are the reason the authors give for brachytherapy lacking any urethral consensus. Cross-series comparison here supports feasibility, not a ranking of modalities.

The oncologic trade-off is the question the review is candid about without resolving. Sparing the urethra below prescription risks underdosing periurethral disease. The reassurance offered, that the urethral-sparing trials showed no suggestion of high relapse rates, comes without event counts or follow-up, which is thin support for de-escalating dose to tissue that can harbour tumor. The authors' own conditions, reliable localisation on MRI or PSMA PET and tumor away from the urethra, are the gating criteria a reader should apply, and they describe a selected subset rather than the typical intermediate-risk gland.

Several clinically actionable points depend less on dosimetry. The ASCENDE-RT stricture excess with brachytherapy boost (18.4% vs 5.2%) is randomised evidence that escalating dose by that route carries a urinary price, which is the trade-off focal EBRT boosting tries to avoid. The anticoagulant bleeding data (15.5% vs 3.6% at 4 years) come from a single institution and are open to confounding by comorbidity, but the direction is plausible and informs counselling. The TURP guidance, pre-emptive before RT for obstructive baseline function and avoided early after RT, rests on small retrospective series and a systematic review the authors concede could not be pooled.

What the review does not settle is whether urethral steering changes patient-reported late urgency in a randomised comparison. The ongoing trials it lists (NINJA, PACE-B, HEAT, NRG GU005) randomise fractionation schedules or boost technique, not urethral constraints, so even when mature they will inform the constraint question only indirectly.

significance_by_specialty.radonc: The planning numbers are the transferable part: urethra D0.1 cm³ <105% of prescription from FLAME, and Dmax <107% at 40 Gy/5 fx tied to an estimated 7.7% late moderate GU rate. Sparing below prescription stays conditional on reliable MRI or PSMA PET localisation with tumor clear of the urethra.
